newsitem.title: USA: First lady describes Clintons' private Christmas.
newsitem.headline: First lady describes Clintons' private Christmas.

text.p: Hillary Rodham Clinton Tuesday provided a rare glimpse into the first family's private Christmas.
The president is a frantic last-minute "mallstalker," and their daughter, Chelsea, is busy finishing her college applications, Mrs. Clinton revealed.

The Clintons this week concluded two weeks of exhausting official celebrations featuring daily receptions, tours and parties at the White House and turned to their personal Christmas rituals and celebrations.

"We celebrate privately on the second and third floors of the White House. Our own 17-foot tree goes up in the Yellow Oval Room, right above the official tree that stands in the Blue Room downstairs," Hillary Clinton wrote in her syndicated column, "Talking It Over."
A copy of the column, which will appear in subscribing newspapers Wednesday, was released by Creators Syndicate Inc.
Mrs. Clinton said the family, including visiting relatives and, for the first time, baby nephews Tyler and Zachary, was "rushing madly about" to finish Christmas preparations.
The tree was put up a few days ago and decorated with boxes of ornaments collected over the years. Following family tradition, President Clinton added the finishing touches.

"Another ritual for Bill is a last-minute shopping trip to the mall," Mrs. Clinton wrote. "I have noticed over the years that many men of my acquaintance become frantic mallstalkers as they hunt for Chrismas gifts. ... I'm sure my husband gives the same joy to sales clerks today."
The president did, indeed, embark on a last-minute shopping expedition Tuesday afternoon, his second in as many days.
After a soggy round of golf with his brother-in-law, Tony Rodham, at the Army-Navy Country Club, Clinton braved steady rain to slip into the Pentagon City Mall through a side door.

Amazed and delighted shoppers loaded with bags and children followed him and his Secret Service escort as he browsed in the windows of Scribner's bookstore, the Wentworth Gallery and other stores in the upscale shopping centre.
Ethiopian immigrant Eyassu Teklu presented Clinton with an early Christmas gift, unexpectedly stopping the president and handing him a CD called "Elemental Rhythm and Blues."
"I told him I was an Ethiopian and as an immigrant loved him very much," said the 38-year-old Teklu, an Alexandria, Va., resident who came to the United States 18 years ago.
Later the Clintons honoured another family tradition by watching their 16-year-old daughter dance in a production of "The Nutcracker," this one by the Washington Ballet.

"We have done this every year since she was three," Mrs. Clinton wrote in her column. She noted that "between decorating and pirouetting," Chelsea had the added experience this year of finishing her college applications, due early next month.
"She's been at the computer trying to write essays that explain -- in 500 words -- who she is. ... Bill and I are still trying to persuade her to stay in Washington and take correspondence courses."

The Clintons and their extended family traditionally have Christmas Eve dinner with Vernon Jordan, a close friend and adviser; his wife, Ann; and their children and grandchildren. Then they attend a service at the National Cathedral.
"When we finally arrive back at the White House around midnight, we'll finish wrapping our gifts and stuffing our stockings," Mrs. Clinton wrote.
